newsitem.title: USA: Moody's says cuts Norfolk, Va., GOs to A1 from Aa.
newsitem.headline: Moody's says cuts Norfolk, Va., GOs to A1 from Aa.

text.p: Norfolk's general obligation bond rating has been lowered from Aa to A1 with a stable outlook in connection with its upcoming sale of $48,175,000 bonds scheduled for competitive bids on April 24.
The rating change is based on the city's continuing trend of slow economic and revenue growth which has contributed to tightened financial operations and weaker liquidity.

Debt position remains manageable, although debt levels have been increasing and are above average. Norfolk remains an important regional economic center for Hampton Roads with a large institutional and military presence. The city maintains good budgetary control over finances which should lead to stable results.
Also, the city's above average rate of bond retirement, coupled with expected reductions in its annual tax-supported borrowing over the next several years, should keep debt position manageable.

Important Economic Center for Hampton Roads Despite Inherent Weaknesses A considerable military presence dominates Norfolk's economy, although the city is also considered the traditional business and health care center for the region.The city is actively attempting to broaden its mature economy to reverse negative population trends.

A major initiative by city officials is the redevelopment of the downtown area using public and private investment. Private sources are being leveraged with loans and grants from the city and other levels of government.

A major $300 million regional shopping mall is currently being built as a cornerstone for downtown redevelopment. Despite these efforts, Norfolk's population and income levels versus the state, have been declining since 1970. Tightly Balanced Financial Operations Norfolk's financial operations remain satisfactory but tightly balanced.

Finances are supported by a slowly growing tax base and large portion of intergovernmental aid for schools. Operating flexiblity is hampered by comparative high property tax rates and small increases in assessed valuation. Other taxes are also growing relatively slowly.

General Fund balance is at satisfactory levels, but liquidity has weakened. The city has completed a multi-year consolidation program which reduced municipal employee levels by 17% through attrition. But because of the city's increased needs for schools, public safety, economic and community development, further operating efficiencies will be difficult to achieve.

Manageable Above Average Debt Position Debt levels are above average and payout is rapid. Future tax-supported borrowing requirements appear manageable. A quarter of general obligation debt is self-supporting from the strong water and sewer utilities.

Debt service makes a moderate though increasing claim on General Fund revenues. The city is using its debt capacity to leverage economic development efforts. This includes $57 million general obligation bonds issued for a maritime attraction that has not been self-supporting, and recently $55 million parking revenue bonds for the new regional shopping center.

The parking revenue bonds will be secured by system revenues, ahead of $31 million general obligation parking bonds now being paid from that revenue source. The city expects revenues from the expanded parking system will be sufficient to pay all bonds.

Also, at this time, we are assigning a MIG 1 rating to Norfolk's General Obligation Bond Anticipation Notes (Taxable) Series 1997 also selling on April 24. The $2 million Series 1997 BANs, which will finance public health facilities, are dated April 24, 1997 and mature April 24, 1998. General Obligation Bonds Outstanding after this sale is $556.6 million.
